other_side: Zitron opens his piece with the Astra launch itself, but not to argue about benchmarks: his point is that the 'AGI has arrived' chorus from Jensen Huang, Greg Brockman and a compliant press is a distraction from financials that do not add up. He cites Ramp data that 80 per cent of OpenAI and Anthropic's enterprise revenue comes from 1 per cent of customers, heavily AI start-ups burning venture capital on tokens, and notes that every new model launch produces a revenue surge precisely because those start-ups must offer 'the latest models at whatever cost'. In his framing an 'opportunity model' with no established use cases is exactly what a bubble produces: a spectacle of capability, funded by borrowed money, ahead of at least two hundred billion dollars of compute commitments falling due next year.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether a new capability set turns into paid, durable demand before the money behind it runs out. Both accept as fact that Astra does things earlier models could not, notably computer use and 3D, that the weekend's tests were a poor fit for it, and that revenue spikes around launches. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the spike persists: the observable is OpenAI's and Anthropic's revenue mix a year on, specifically whether the share from non-tech, non-start-up enterprises has risen. The worldview residue is whether spectacle without a use case is early or hollow. NLW is vindicated if computer use becomes an ordinary paid workflow in firms that are not themselves AI companies; Zitron if the Ramp concentration figure is unchanged when the 2027 compute bills arrive. Both are polemicists with incentives, one bullish and anti-doom, the other bubble-certain and anti-hype, and they agree nobody yet knows what Astra is for. Watch the customer concentration number, not the benchmarks.
